episodes.212756: During the 17th evening into the 18th early morning, a strong upper-level disturbance interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable airmass across central and southern Indiana. Strong vertical wind shear and moderate atmospheric instability supported the rapid development of supercells and bowing linear segments capable of producing tornadoes, damaging straight-line winds, and torrential rainfall.||Severe weather initiated in western Indiana around 7:40 PM EST on June 17 and tracked southeastward across the state through 1:25 AM EST on June 18. Four tornadoes touched down during the outbreak, highlighted by a strong EF-3 tornado with peak winds of 140 mph that tracked over 18 miles across Owen and Monroe counties, causing severe structural damage to residential properties and widespread tree damage. Three additional EF-1 tornadoes, with peak winds ranging between 95 mph and 110 mph, caused localized structural and timber damage across Vigo, Clay, Brown, and Jackson counties.||In addition to tornadoes, widespread straight-line wind gusts between 58 mph and 70 mph caused scattered tree and power line damage across broad portions of central and southern Indiana, resulting in temporary road blockages and localized power outages. Intense rainfall rates accompanying the initial severe thunderstorms also produced localized flash flooding in Vigo County, leading to multiple road closures in and around Terre Haute. This severe weather event would be the fifth of many for the month which would eventually define a formal disaster period from June 6th to the 18th which was declared by the governor of Indiana.

By June 20, the stalled front over Central Alabama reignited training thunderstorms along the U.S. 280 and I-22 corridors, with heavy rainfall of 2 to 5 inches causing flash flooding in the Birmingham metro area during the afternoon hours.

episodes.214016: A summer pattern of south to southwestern mean flow, combined with impacts from both the Gulf and Atlantic sea breezes and PWATs near or above 2 inches, resulted in numerous thunderstorms across northeast FL.

An isolated severe storm embedded in a line led to isolated wind damage.
episodes.214349: A strong and persistent warm air advection pattern atop a surface front fostered scattered thunderstorm activity for most of the morning into the afternoon on the 18th across north-central Oklahoma. Sufficient wind shear and (elevated) instability allowed for occasional large hail concern with the strongest thunderstorms. Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall across Grant County, Oklahoma also led to flooding.
episodes.214546: Several rounds of significant convection impacted central Illinois on June 17th, 2026.  Clusters of thunderstorms initially formed on the nose of a strong low-level jet streak across Iowa during the pre-dawn hours, then tracked southeastward along a warm frontal boundary into central Illinois through midday. Scattered damaging wind gusts were reported in north-central Illinois, with the most concentrated corridor of 60-70 mph winds focused along a Galesburg, to Peoria, to Chenoa line.||Thunderstorms re-developed along a remnant outflow boundary from the morning convection by mid to late afternoon, with the most intense cells materializing along and south of a Springfield to Paris line where several tornadoes occurred and hail larger than baseballs (3 diameter) was reported across portions of Moultrie, Douglas, and Coles counties. An EF2 tornado impacted the Mattoon to Charleston area, and an EF3 tracked just north of Effingham.
episodes.214547: A mid-level low pressure system associated with Post-Tropical Storm Arthur pushed slowly through the area resulting in several rounds of thunderstorms over the coastal waters.  Some of these storms produced strong downburst winds over the waters resulting in several marine thunderstorm wind events.
episodes.214551: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in several tornadoes impacting the Houma and New Orleans metro areas.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas including the cities of Houma, Kenner, and Slidell.  Another area of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms formed over central Louisiana near the center of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur producing flash flooding in portions of Pointe Coupee Parish.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 19th.  This activity was focused in metro New Orleans where a brief EF-0 tornado developed in the community of Arabi.  On June 20th, another band of thunderstorms developed along a lingering boundary stretching from coastal Louisiana toward New Orleans.  This band of thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and  impacted portions of the Houma and New Orleans metro areas producing a few flash flooding events in Houma, Destrehan, and Kenner.
episodes.214562: A mesoscale convective system formed on the eastern side of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur on June 18th.  Favorable low level winds allowed for multiple mini-supercells to form on the leading edge of the mesoscale convective system resulting in a few tornadoes affecting coastal Mississippi.  These tornadoes were rated as EF-0 and EF-1 events.  A bow echo also developed over coastal Mississippi leading to severe winds and thunderstorm wind damage in the Gulfport-Biloxi metro area.  Additionally, the mesoscale convective complex tapped into a region of deep tropical moisture with atmospheric moisture content well above normal levels for mid-June.  This resulted in several significant flash flooding events in portions of coastal Mississippi including the city of Picayune.  Two fatalities occurred near Picayune where rainfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour and QPE of 10 to 15 inches was noted.  This very high rainfall total resulted in major flooding on the West Hobolochitto Creek on June 18th and this is where the fatalities occurred.  Lingering moisture and weak upper level troughing associated with the slow moving remnants of Post-Tropical Storm Arthur produced additional thunderstorm activity on June 20th.  This activity was focused in Biloxi where additional flash flooding occurred.
episodes.214613: A cold front brought severe weather, heavy rain, and flash flooding to southeast Alabama.
episodes.214656: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 18-22 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported along with flash flooding.
episodes.214784: Low pressure tracking across Quebec province drew an occluding front across the region through the afternoon and evening of the 18th. A strong low level jet crossed Downeast portions of the region in advance of the front. Convective showers and isolated thunderstorms along the front broke the inversion allowing the stronger winds aloft to mix down to the surface. Wind gusts estimated at up to 60 mph occurred. Numerous trees were downed along the convective line of showers and isolated thunderstorms across southern Penobscot county including the Bangor region. Saturated ground from earlier heavy rains allowed trees to be more easily toppled.|Trees and branches falling on power lines led to scattered power outages. Gusty winds and saturated ground also allowed some trees to be toppled in advance of the convective line which also contributed to power outages.
episodes.215007: Scattered severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds across northern Ohio.
episodes.215056: A cluster of thunderstorms developed within the vicinity of a strong mid-upper level shortwave trough and a surface low. One supercell tracked from southeast Minnesota through northeast Iowa and into southwest Wisconsin while maintaining is strength during the late afternoon. The storm evolved into a line as it trtacked through south central Wisconsin during the early evening and produced a swath of damaging winds and three tornadoes.
episodes.215071: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a cold front from the northwest maintained their strength to deliver damaging wind gusts resulting in downed trees and power lines across southeast West Virginia. In spite of the early morning hours, there was Effective Bulk Shear of 30-40 kts and a few hundred MLCAPE to keep the system alive. These storms dissipated after crossing the Appalachian mountains and encountering relatively stable air.
episodes.215072: A line of thunderstorms that passed over the mountains earlier in the day reorganized and strengthened to become severe thunderstorms later in the evening in North Carolina. A few notable cells travelled west to east just south of the VA/NC border and brought numerous trees and power lines down. This part of the forecast area had notable deep moisture convergence and CAPE of about 1000-2000 J/kg. Lapse rates were underwhelming at the low level and mid-level, but bulk shear of 30-40 knots allowed sufficient storm organization and intensification to deliver several damaging wind gusts.
episodes.215073: Storms following the Appalachian mountains reorganized later in the afternoon and brought damaging wind gusts to parts of south-central Virginia. Surface heating and mixing resulted in MLCAPE values of 750-1000 J/kg and low level lapse rates of 7-8��C/km. Mid-level lapse rates were not as impressive which may have limited the coverage of severe storms but DCAPE values of 700-900 J/kg contributed to some downed trees in Charlotte and Halifax Counties.
episodes.215093: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed eastern New York on June 18, 2026. Gusty winds ahead of a complex of showers and thunderstorms produced some incidents of downed trees, mainly in eastern Schenectady and Washington counties. The passing line of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. Some of these trees and wires fell onto residences. This knocked out power to some areas, some of which remained without power into June 19, 2026.
episodes.215094: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed southern Vermont on June 18, 2026. A complex of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and wires as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours. One of these trees fell onto a private residence.
episodes.215095: An anomalously strong low pressure system and frontal system crossed western Massachusetts on June 18, 2026. A complex of showers and thunderstorms downed trees and large branches as it crossed through the area during the afternoon hours.
episodes.215139: A cold front across the lower Ohio valley moved into North Carolina and led to the development of widespread showers and storms in the middle to late evening hours. Numerous damaging wind reports were observed.
episodes.215520: On June 18, 2026, an approaching upper-level shortwave trough and associated cold front crossed the NWS Buffalo region, interacting with a developing warm sector to trigger scattered showers and severe thunderstorms. According to NWS Buffalo Area Forecast Discussions, early-morning clouds and showers along a warm front initially limited heating, but afternoon boundary-layer destabilization yielded 1,000 to 1,500 J/kg of MUCAPE���particularly across the Western Southern Tier. The Storm Prediction Center outlined a Marginal Risk for severe weather, noting that 0���6 km bulk shear values near 45 knots and steep low-level lapse rates would support multi-cell storm structures capable of producing localized damaging wind gusts. Meanwhile, the Weather Prediction Center noted a subdued flash flood threat; although warm-cloud depth and precipitable water values over 1.25 inches fueled heavy downpours, fast storm motion kept rainfall progressive enough to prevent widespread flooding. Following the cold frontal passage, convective activity waned overnight as cooler air over Lake Erie initiated early-season lake effect rain bands and a lingering potential for waterspouts.
episodes.215551: A cluster of thunderstorms moved east through northern West Virginia on the periphery of an MCS diving through Kentucky in the early morning hours. Despite the unfavorable timing, weak MLCAPE values of 250-500 J/kg was enough when coupled with strong effective shear values of 50-70 knots beneath a seasonably very strong 90-100 knot mid-level jet to support sporadic wind damage in northern West Virginia.
episodes.215563: A Mesoscale Convective System moved across the Ohio Valley on the night of June 17th, 2026 and the morning of June 18th, 2026. Supercells congealed into a line of storms as it moved south into southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. These storms brought severe winds and a few tornadoes to the area. Additionally, long residence time of heavy rainfall lead to flash flooding that lasted through most of the day on June 18th, 2026.
episodes.215597: A very subtle disturbance in deep northwest flow helped to fire a thunderstorm around El Paso.  A very dry surface with dew point depressions of over 60 degrees contributed to a wind gust to 67 mph at KELP.

episodes.215667: Remnants from Tropical Storm Arthur produced heavy rain that caused flash flooding, including some significant flash flooding, across portions of central and southern Mississippi. Multiple roads were flooded in the area and several cars had become stranded.

episodes.215695: A small cluster of storms moved eastward across interior southern Virginia well ahead of cold front on June 18. This cluster produced a swath of damaging winds.

episodes.215717: An upper level trough was moving southeast through southern New Mexico with some mid level moisture available for thunderstorms to develop. events.narrative: Trees and powerlines were blown down on Route 104 between Taylorville and Kincaid.
Property and tree damage occurred at Ashmore Estates.

Tornado began west of a farm in an open field and moved east southeast through the northern portion of Belleville.  Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted.  Peeled shingles and siding as well as damage to soffit and guttering on several homes. A garage on one home fell in after its roof was lifted.  A garage on another home was breached at the garage door and the structure failed, peeling downwind and taking a large portion of the dwelling's roof decking.  The tornado continued east southeast over a farm field damaging corn and a long water sprinkler. The end of the path east of County Road D featured additional trees snapped and uprooted before lifting in the Brooklyn Wildlife Area.
About a mile of powerlines were blown down along IL Rt. 16 from Ashmore eastbound.  Several trees were downed and power poles were snapped as well.
Flash flooding within the Black Wash that impacted a large area of the Pasqua Yaqui Tribe land.

Video of a brief tornado shared with Lafayette County Emergency Management shows a narrow tornado occurring near the East Branch of the Pecatonica River south of Argyle. In the video, some tree branches and limbs are hit or downed.  Storm survey wasn't able to yield any additional damage points.
Social media videos showed a well-defined funnel cloud southeast of Letohatchee. No contact with the ground was evident via radar and no ground reports were received.
A creek flowed out of its banks, resulting in three feet of water across a road.
Swift water rescue reported near Elm St and N Stone Rd. Nearby rainfall gauges recorded between 0.5 and 0.75 inches of rainfall. No injuries or fatalities reported.
A peak wind gust to 67 mph was recorded at the El Paso Airport.
The roofs of a couple businesses were blown off in downtown Marshall near Rt. 1 and Archer Ave.

Swift water rescue reported for two individuals in the Santa Cruz River, with one fatality and two injuries. MRMS Multi-Sensor estimated between 1.0-1.5 inches of rainfall fell in multiple locations nearby.
The Silver City AWOS recorded a peak gust of 61 mph.
The Biggs Air Field ASOS recorded a peak gust of 61 mph.
Trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds.
Large tree downed by thunderstorm wind gusts on Meridian Line Road.

An EF-1 tornado with path length of 6.64 miles and a path width of 300 yards began in eastern Vigo County. Within Vigo county the peak width was 75 yards, path length of 2.14 miles and peak winds of 95 mph. The peak winds were 110 mph after it moved into Clay county. Damage within Vigo county was limited to tree damage along East Dallas Drive.
A severe thunderstorm produced hail ranging from nickel to half dollar sized along with strong winds.

An EF-1 tornado with path length of 6.64 miles and a path width of 300 yards began in eastern Vigo County before moving into Clay county. Within Clay county the peak width was 300 yards, path length of 4.5 miles and peak winds of 110 mph. Damage within Clay county included significant damage to a 100 year old brick barn and several homesteads in western Clay county along 200S.
An NMDOT Mesonet site at mile marker 7 recorded a peak gust of 59 mph.

As the tornado tracked further along E 1700th Ave, it damaged |another outbuilding, two grain bins and additional trees before |finally lifting approximately 0.25 miles east of N 800th St.
Trees were blown down by thunderstorm winds.
Numerous roads closed due to flooding in Terre Haute and points to the south in Vigo County.
N Santa Rita Ave became impassible with a measured 6 inches of water moving across roadway. An estimated 0.5 to 0.75 inches of rainfall recorded nearby.
A brief tornado touched down in rural Jasper County, about 2.5 miles southwest of Rose Hill. Tree damage was noted along N 1050th St, with trunks snapped on several hardwood trees.
A trained spotter and storm chaser shared video of a brief tornado about 3 miles southeast of Rose Hill.  There was no damage noted in this rural part of the county.

An EF-3 tornado with path length of at 18.49 miles and maximum width of 880 yards began in eastern Owen county. The peak winds were 140 mph, but within Owen county the maximum width was 250 yards with peak winds of 85 mph making it officially an EF-0 for the county. Damage was sporadic with several trees damaged and 1 structure impacted.
A 15 inch diameter tree was downed by thunderstorm wind gusts along with shingle damage.

An EF-3 tornado with path length of at 18.49 miles and maximum width of 880 yards moved through much of Monroe county after exiting Owen county.. The peak winds were 140 mph. Drone footage showed a widespread path through mostly forested area with several areas of widespread debarking of the trees. The tornado impacted and destroyed several homes along Bowman and Mount Pleasant Road with the most intense damage along Buskirk road. An EF-1 tornado with path length of 6.35 miles and a maximum width of 325 yards moved through portions of Jackson county. The peak winds were 110 mph with the tornado impacting mostly heavily wooded areas and a few residences.

The first damage produced by the tornado occurred on Texas Gas Road, where a large tree was uprooted and other smaller trees were downed. Farther east along Cole Lane, an attached garage was destroyed and a large tree was downed onto a house. In addition, a roof was lifted from another garage and several trees were snapped at their trunks. ||The tornado strengthened and proceeded east near East Laughery Creek Road, where it completely destroyed a house and two outbuildings. Debris from these buildings was strewn east along the path of the tornado across a large field. Based on this damage, estimated wind speeds were around 130 mph in this area, and the damage also resulted in a Tornadic Debris Signature on the Wilmington, Ohio radar at this time. ||The tornado continued toward Alta Vista Ave, where a large number of hardwood trees were snapped. The tornado developed in Dearborn County at 2314EST on Texas Gas Road, about 4 miles east of Dillsboro. An EF-0 tornado touched down near Bayou la Cache, east of Chauvin, LA in Terrebonne Parish and tracked northeast toward Montegut, LA. High resolution satellite imagery depicted a defined swath of tree damage beginning over inaccessible areas which aligned with a tornado debris signature on Climavision V014. The damage path grew to a maximum width of 200 yards and peaked in intensity over inaccessible forest west of Blue Jay St as it enroached on neighborhoods near Crochetville Rd. The tornado gradually weakened and decreased in size as it moved over southern parts of Montegut, near Crochetville Rd where mainly minor tree damage was noted. It is estimated that this tornado dissipated near Willow Aly and Bayou Terrebonne.

A well-defined damage path of an EF-0 tornado was identified on high-resolution satellite imagery over rural, inaccessible parts of southeast St. Charles Parish. The tornado touched down near Bayou des Allemands and tracked north-northwest over rural, inaccessible marshland. While the majority of damage along this path was marsh vegetation, a narrow swath of trees were evidently damaged/displaced which is the basis for its EF-0 rating. The tornado continued north-northwest with the narrow damage path becoming less defined with time. The tornado dissipated east of Bayou Gauche after being on the ground for over 3 miles.

The National Weather Service completed a storm survey and determined that a tornado occurred during the early morning hours on June 18, 2026 in Scott County and Jefferson County Indiana and then crossed the river into Trimble County Kentucky. Predominantly minor to moderate patches of tree damage were visible on high resolution satellite imagery along its path which were collocated with a tornado debris signature on Climavision radar V014. Trees were more evidently displaced and damaged as the tornado exited the inaccessible marsh and forested areas and moved over Crozier Drive. A NWS survey team observed two homes on Crozier Drive that had significant roof loss and at least one exterior wall collapsed for both homes. The tornado continued northeast across Bayou Dularge Rd and into more inaccessible marsh and forest vegetation where more minor damage was evident on satellite imagery. The end point of this tornado is estimated and it's possible it extended further northeast though no conclusive evidence of damage was identified.

State Route 690 was closed due to flooding and State Route 681 was closed due to flooding beyond Hebbardsville Road. Several areas of flooding were observed in Athens with vehicles stuck in flood waters.

The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred on Union Hill Road, about six tenths of a mile north of Appalachian Highway, where a few hardwood trees were snapped and multiple limbs were broken off of trees. The tornado then moved through a heavily forested area towards the intersection of Lansing Road and Chenoweth Fork Road where more tree damage was noted. Tree damage continued in a concentrated path to the east-northeast along Chenoweth Fork Road before crossing Appalachian Highway and causing a fair amount of tree damage at a rest station on Meads Road. The damage noted in the first third of the tornado's path consisted of broken branches, snapped trunks, and uprooted mature trees. This was consistent with EF-0 and EF-1 damage. ||The tornado continued east through a forest with a large hillside that was not accessible by ground survey. This coincided with the first evidence of a Tornadic Debris Signature on the Wilmington, Ohio radar. When the tornado came down the ridgeline just west of Elm Grove, the most significant damage indicators were noted. An entire section of hardwood forest, about 200-250 yards wide, was blown down. Drone photography and the ground survey confirmed all hardwood trees in this location were snapped, with none left standing. The estimate for this type of tree damage was around 115 mph, consistent with low end EF-2 damage.  ||Some higher-end EF-1 damage was observed as the tornado moved northeast off the hillside into Elm Grove, where the complete collapse of out buildings and barns occurred. Additionally, a significant portion of a roof off was lifted off of a house and large power transmission lines were snapped. After Elm Grove, the tornado turned southeast and caused additional damage near the intersection of State Route 772 and Appalachian Highway. The final evidence of tree damage was located on Sun Fish Creek Road, about a half mile south of Tennyson Road.

A NWS survey team concluded an EF-1 tornado tracked from Evelyn Ave towards Woodhaven Dr and Roberta Grove Blvd. Several businesses in the Lynn Park Shopping Center (at the corner of Prospect Ave and Grand Caillou Rd) sustained damage to almost every window and had partially collapsed interior walls and their roof. HVAC equipment on the roof was thrown northward onto the ground from these businesses. 4 homes had partial to significant roof loss. One home had an exterior wall collapsed. The first evidence of tornadic damage occurred on a property just east of Clarks Creek where several trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado would continue east towards Baton Rouge Road, where several more hardwood trees had large branches broken off, with tree debris thrown onto both sides of the road. Additionally, a barn was completely destroyed in the same area. Sporadic tree damage continued along Baton Rouge Road, eventually leading to another barn where the walls completely collapsed and the roof was blown off. The damage to these outbuildings was consistent with |EF-1 damage, with maximum winds around 90 mph. Just a bit farther down the road, another outbuilding had its sheet metal roof completely ripped off, with pieces of sheet metal thrown about 50 yards into the nearby field. Some of the siding was also peeled off. ||The damage continued along portions of Baton Rouge Road, with extensive tree damage noted leading up to the intersection of Interstate 75. Most of the tree damage was primarily large branches that were broken off, but there was one hardwood tree that was uprooted. Just east of Interstate 75, additional tree and power pole damage occurred. ||The area of most concentrated damage occurred in several neighborhoods just east of U.S. Route 25. On Ridgelea Drive, there were multiple large, healthy trees that were uprooted and/or snapped at the base. On Humes Ridge Road, more large trees and wooden power poles were snapped. The most significant damage occurred near the end of the tornadic path on Waterworks Road, where a standalone, multi-car garage had the majority of its roof ripped off. Multiple sections of the garage had significant loss of its cinder block exterior walls, as well as some minor damage to the interior walls between car ports. Debris from the garage was spread out into the nearby field. Given the structural integrity of the garage, it was estimated that wind speeds up to 95 mph were observed in this part of the tornado track,| consistent with EF-1 damage. The National Weather Service conducted a damage survey across portions of Pendleton County. The survey team noted extensive tree damage across the southern half of the county. Some of the more significant damage occurred near several neighborhoods south of Falmouth, where numerous trees were uprooted/snapped at the base, along with structural damage to several homes and outbuildings. Most of the observed damage from these buildings was a loss of roofing material, but there were a couple of outbuildings that had collapsed walls that led to a complete failure of the structure.|This type of damage is consistent with winds of 80-85 mph. There was additional tree damage in western portions of the county, as well as southeastern portions near McKinneysburg. When overlaying all of this damage with radar imagery, the likely cause of this damage was from straight-line winds as an enhanced surge in the winds created a bowing segment feature on radar, with the apex of this bow moving through the southern half of Pendleton County.

A National Weather Service damage survey concluded that a brief EF-0 touched down early on the morning of Thursday June 18th, 2026. The brief spin-up tornado was embedded within a larger swath of sporadic straight-line wind damage, and touched down about 3 miles due west of Cynthiana between Mill Creek and Mill Creek Meadows Drive. Here, some tree damage as well as roof damage to a metal barn were sustained. Winds were estimated to be 80 mph with this damage. The tornado then traveled east of Mill Creek Meadows Drive toward Ammerman Pike doing more tree damage and scattering some roofing material from the upstream barn. At Ammerman Pike and|Highway 356, another metal barn sustained roof damage and had side panels blown out, along with some roof and fascia damage to a home. A large softwood tree was also uprooted here. Peak winds at this location were rated at 85 mph as the tornado made a hard northward turn and dissipated north of the Highway 356 and Ammerman Pike intersection. The tornado was on the ground for 1 minute or less and traveled less than three quarters of a mile. Peak width was estimated at 80 yards wide.

An NWS Storm Survey determined that a swath of straight line wind damage occurred on the morning of June 18th. Most of the damage occurred near the intersection of Poplar Level Road and Fern Valley Road where a warehouse building roof was partially |collapsed, a small building lost some roofing material, and a tree was downed. The collapsed roof was pancaked downward with no debris lifted or thrown downstream. In addition, some insulation from the roof collapse was laying on the north side of the |building, but not scattered downwind. The orientation of the tree damage was NW to SE, and consistent with TDWR velocity data showing a wind surge from WNW to ESE. Severe level wind gusts were measured with this velocity surge upstream of the damage as well.||Sporadic tree damage also occurred to the ESE of the initial damage point along Fegenbush Lane. Damage stopped just north of Luhr Elementary School after a 1.25 mile swath of sporadic damage.||There had been a supercell thunderstorm that passed through the area about 15 minutes prior, however the TSDF TDWR noted no low level rotational couplet with the radar beam at 200-300 feet AGL. Some mid level rotation was noted off of LVX, but at a higher overall height. Both radar data and damage patterns, as well as an eyewitness account just after 5 AM all pointed more toward the second straight line wind signature as the culprit.||A second area of damage was also surveyed in Fern Creek along Volney Ct. Here, a large branch from a healthy large tree fell into the corner bedroom of a home. Luckily, occupants inside where shaken, but not injured. It was determined that this damage|occurred just before Midnight, well before any thunderstorms arrived. This damage was attributed to non-thunderstorm gradient winds. Nearby observations at from the KLOU ASOS at Bowman Field did measure a 44 MPH gust around the time the residents said the damage occurred.

The tornado began just west of Martha Comer Drive, snapping several hardwood tree trunks before moving across the southern portion of a community college campus. The Kentucky Mesonet site on campus measured a wind gust of 114 mph. The tornado then tracked east and northeast across open field, eventually hitting several businesses along Kentucky Highway 9 (AA Highway), causing roof and structural damage. As the tornado approached East Maple Leaf Road, it quickly intensified. A couple of residences were severely damaged, including an outbuilding demolished with pieces and contents of the structure thrown between 100 to 200 feet. This included a 690 pound four wheeler and a large cinder block. A dual axle trailer jacked up on a block was pushed nearly 100 feet before being stopped by a cement barrier. A house suffered extensive roof damage. A property on the east side of East Maple Leaf Road was also heavily damaged with the debris in a convergent path. This included the roof and siding of a house, several snapped and uprooted hardwood trees, and a couple of hardwood fences that were posted well into the ground, that were pulled toward the circulation. Splatter was observed on the east and south sides of the home, further suggesting a cyclonic rotation. |The tornado then took a left turn toward the northeast as it snapped more trees and destroyed another portion of a fence. Additionally, on the southern side of the tornado, a couple of large barns were heavily damaged with both roofs a total loss, as outflow winds occurred on the south side of the tornado. As the tornado continued on a northeast track across a field, a metal outbuilding was pulled down a hill as the circulation neared. Additional tree damage was observed east of Hill City Road before the tornado dissipated. Sporadic tree damage was reported farther northeast toward the Ohio River as a result of outflow winds.

NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado impacted areas near Bayou Cane and moved northeast across US Hwy 190 west of Lacombe, LA in St. Tammany Parish. The tornado touched down near the shore of Lake Pontchartrain or came ashore as a tornadic waterspout with evident damage to marsh vegetation and trees per high resolution satellite imagery. The tornado was at peak intensity west of Lemieux Blvd where ground surveyors observed a few snapped trees on Cane Bayou Access Trail. Additional tree damage occurred on private property including several uprooted trees and a few snapped trunks as well as visible damage to a shed. The tornado uprooted and partially snapped trees as it crossed the Tammany Trace Bike Trail. The tornado began to evidently weaken as it approached and crossed US Hwy 190 causing only minor tree damage north of the highway. The tornado is estimated to have lifted near Azalea St and Cane Bayou Ln.

An EF-1 tornado tracked across parts of St. Charles and Jefferson Parishes, affecting the community of Avondale, LA. This tornado began over the Salvador Wildlife Management Area as evidenced by a well-defined 15-20 yard wide path of damage to marsh vegetation oriented southwest to northeast that was collocated with an intensifying area of rotation on both TMSY and KHDC. This damage path gradually broadened and fluctuated in intensity causing minor damage to trees as it traveled over uninhabited and inaccessible marsh areas. The tornado damage path evidently became larger and more noticeable again near Bayou Verret. A clear path of tree damage was evident on high resolution satellite imagery spanning to approximately 300 yards wide with numerous trees damaged or displaced as the tornado exited St Charles Parish and crossed into Jefferson Parish 1.35 miles south of Highway 90 along Bayou Verret.

An EF-1 tornado entered Jefferson Parish from St. Charles Parish 1.35 miles south of Highway 90 near over inaccessible areas to ground survey team near the levees along Bayou Verret. A clear path of tree damage was evident on high resolution satellite imagery spanning to at least 250 yards wide with numerous trees displaced. The damage path within this inaccessible area became weaker and less apparent as the tornado approached US Hwy 90. The tornado was at EF-0 intensity as it crossed US Hwy 90 into Avondale. As it tracked northeast, the tornado caused light home damage and snapped tree branches. The tornado restrengthened to low-end EF-1 intensity at George Street, rolling a single-wide manufactured home into another home which was the cause of the most significant structural damage. The manufactured home was thrown to the northeast with the frame being well bent. 2 people were injured as a result. Additional home damage was also found on Defourneaux Ln as the tornado began to weaken again. It's estimated that the tornado lifted after crossing Restlawn Park Cemetery, near Center Street.

A brief EF0 tornado touched down in Eden Isle, LA and moved east. Widespread branches and tree debris was found in Eden Isle along with a few houses with minor damage. One house had a failure at the garage where the wind looks to have been pushed into the garage. The tornado damaged businesses right near I-10 as it crossed over with a few more homes damaged and trees down in Lakeshore Village. The widespread light damage across Eden Isle did make this a difficult track, especially track width, to find. The additional damage was likely inflow from straight line winds and/or debris that was swirling out of the tornado.

NWS ground survey confirmed an EF-1 tornado with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph.  The tornado began near or before moving into Treasure Isle where it flipped a large boat on its side. Additional visible damage to homes and lofting of outdoor fixtures was noted as the tornado moved into Martin Drive. The tornado reached EF-1 intensity near Bluegill Drive where it removed shingles off of homes, snapped a few trees, and collapsed garage door structures and blew out a wall or two as a result in two different homes. A defined damage path was observed on LA Hwy 433 and then crossed into inaccesible marsh areas. A weak tornado debris signature was evident on KHDC and is the basis for connecting this damage to Avery Estates. The tornado continued northeast into Avery Estates where minor metal roof damage and tree damage was noted on Avery Drive and Smokey Hollow Drive. The tornado evidently strengthened and grew in size to around 300 yards in width as it moved just south of the northern part of Avery Drive and into US Hwy 190 where numerous trees were uprooted or snapped. Several outbuildings were damaged and tension cables on a cell tower were snapped. It's possible the tornado slowed in this area as it pivoted and turned more to the east per KHDC radar imagery. Along US Hwy 190 a manufactured home had most of its roof removed and it was shifted significantly off its foundation. The tornado then moved into Pearl River Basin, inaccessible to ground survey. The tornado evidently maintained strength or even strengthened further over this area, evidenced by the deepening of a tornado debris signature lofted over 5000 feet. The tornado exited St. Tammany Parish, entering Hancock County in Mississippi north of the town of Pearlington.

The first microburst occurred over the open water of  Lake Winnipesaukee shortly after 4:00 PM on June 18th. Based on damage reports this likely occurred in the vicinity of Round and Welch Islands in Gilford, New Hampshire. There were pictures of trees snapped on Round Island and reported damage on parts of Welch Island. The microburst continued unimpeded by friction towards Sandy and Cow Islands in Tuftonboro, New Hampshire. There were at least three camps damaged by tree falls on Sandy Island. On the southwest side of Cow Island there was significant tree damage. At least three additional camps were damaged by falling trees, as well as at least two docks that sustained damage. An estimated 1,500 trees, mostly softwood, were either snapped or uprooted by the winds. The open water and lack of friction likely allowed this microburst to expand beyond on the accepted definition of areal extent.

It was determined that there was a second microburst just northeast of the first, along the path of the mesocyclone. There was no visible damage to the backlands of Cow |Island, so the NWS Storm Damage Survey Team estimates the second microburst began somewhere just north of Barbers Pole channel before Tuftonboro Neck. This microburst was smaller in areal extent but more intense. Another 1,500 trees, again mostly softwood, were estimated to have been snapped or uprooted. These also caused the majority of the damage observed. There were five vehicles damaged, two of which were total losses. In addition, there were five cabins or outbuildings attached to summer camps that were destroyed and at least another twelve that were damaged by falling trees. Near the Sandy Island Dock several people escaped with minor cuts and scrapes when two trees fell through the shelter they were under. In a nearby parking lot a tree fell onto a car causing one minor hand injury in which medical attention was not necessary.
